message.content: {"4": {"original": "Requests for all but ten of 800+ pages of ACTA draft material to be declassified", "rephrased": "The Electronic Frontier Foundation, a digital rights organization, formally requested that the European Union release the full text of the Anti-Counterfeiting Trade Agreement (ACTA) draft, arguing that withholding 800+ pages of classified material prevented public scrutiny of the deal's impact on civil liberties. Despite these appeals for transparency, the negotiations proceeded under the presidency of George W. Bush, with authorities rebuffing the request to declassify all but ten pages of the document.", "summary": "The Electronic Frontier Foundation demanded full transparency of the secret ACTA draft to ensure public accountability."}, "5": {"original": "asserting that national security concerns justified the entire draft and related", "rephrased": "Following the transition to the Obama administration, the U.S. government maintained its refusal to release the Anti-Counterfeiting Trade Agreement (ACTA) draft, asserting that national security concerns justified keeping the entire document and all related materials secret. This stance continued the policy of secrecy established during the Bush presidency, effectively blocking Freedom of Information requests from activists seeking to understand the agreement's provisions before it was presented to the European Parliament.", "summary": "The Obama administration justified keeping the ACTA draft secret by citing national security concerns."}, "6": {"original": "Protesters feared ACTA's vague wording would cause widespread internet", "rephrased": "Activists and protesters across Europe argued that the Anti-Counterfeiting Trade Agreement (ACTA) contained dangerously vague legal language that would inevitably lead to widespread internet censorship and a severe curtailment of freedom of speech. Furthermore, they warned that the agreement's patent regulations would have potentially adverse impacts on public access to essential medicines and agricultural crop seeds, creating a risk to public health and food security.", "summary": "Activists warned that ACTA's vague terms threatened internet freedom and access to essential medicines."}, "7": {"original": "described the trade agreement as 'giving the U.S. a structural competitive", "rephrased": "Accessnow.org, a global pressure group based in the United States, described the Anti-Counterfeiting Trade Agreement (ACTA) as a mechanism designed to give the U.S. a structural competitive advantage over other nations. The organization highlighted that the agreement had already secured signatories from major economies including Australia, Canada, Japan, and the United States, suggesting the deal was engineered to reinforce American market dominance in global trade.", "summary": "Accessnow.org argued that ACTA was designed to provide the U.S. with a structural trade advantage."}}
